Transient instability and recurrent aggregation in a two–species chemotaxis–competition system under environmental periodicity

Journal: Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena
Federico Herrero-Hervás Email: fedher01@ucm.es Corresponding author: Corresponding author Affiliation: Instituto de Matemática Interdisciplinar, Departamento de Análisis Matemático y Matemática Aplicada, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, 28040, Spain Affiliation: Departamento de Matemática Aplicada, ICAI, Universidad Pontificia de Comillas, Madrid, 28015, Spain    Pedro Hernández-Alonso Affiliation: Departamento de Análisis Matemático y Matemática Aplicada, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, 28040, Spain    Mihaela Negreanu Affiliation: Instituto de Matemática Interdisciplinar, Departamento de Análisis Matemático y Matemática Aplicada, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, 28040, Spain
Abstract

This work investigates recurrent pattern formation in a two–species chemotaxis system with competitive dynamics under the assumption that the carrying capacities of both species are periodic in time. By considering a globally attracting periodic solution to the associated nonautonomous ODE system as a spatially homogeneous base state, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of a critical chemotactic sensitivity of the first species, denoted by χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}. Whenever this threshold is exceeded, the periodic state becomes linearly unstable over a nonempty set of times within each environmental cycle. This gives rise to a recurrent alternation of unstable and stable intervals, during which spatial perturbations are respectively amplified and damped. The analytical derivation is complemented with numerical simulations, in both periodic coexistence and competitive exclusion regimes. Finally, we discuss the temporal location of the instability sets and the possibility of negative instability thresholds.

Keywords:
Chemotaxis, Pattern Formation, Periodicity, Turing Instability, Nonautonomous dynamics

1 Introduction

Periodic dynamics arise in a wide range of natural systems, particularly in ecological communities involving interacting species. Such periodic behavior has been documented in different phenomena ranging from recurrent forest insect outbreaks [7] to cyclic predator–prey dynamics, including the classical lynx-hare interactions [16], arctic rodent populations [21], and different krill species in marine environments [35, 23]. In predator–prey systems, such periodic cycles constitute one of the main features of the classical Lotka–Volterra system, arising in the absence of self-limiting growth effects.

Nevertheless, empirical observation of sustained ecological cycles remains mostly limited, since the available data sets typically span only a few number of oscillations due to the long characteristic timescales involved, which may range from several months to decades. Moreover, in laboratory studies, carried out with fast-reproducing species under controlled constant conditions, sustained periodic oscillations seem particularly difficult to reproduce experimentally. In most cases, the results eventually show either stabilization toward a steady state or extinction of one of the species [29, 43, 45, 18]. From a mathematical perspective, this is consistent with the dynamics of Lotka–Volterra systems incorporating logistic growth terms, with saturation mechanisms effectively suppressing oscillating regimes.

This suggests that persistent population cycles (which have only recently been reproduced experimentally under controlled constant conditions [11, 22]) are either consequence of more complex mechanisms such as intrinsic delays or density-dependent interactions (see for instance [20] and the references therein), or on the contrary, arise from environmental heterogeneity. In the latter case, particularly for environments with strong seasonality effects, substantially more examples have been documented. For instance, it is well known that seasonal changes in temperature, light intensity, salinity and nutrient availability significantly affect plankton populations [39]. In particular, this often leads to phytoplankton blooms, i.e. rapid increases in their population levels [36]. In turn, blooms of harmful phytoplankton species result in a high release of toxins, consequently inducing mass mortality of numerous fish species [12]. In such cases, time-periodic dynamics emerge as a consequence of environmental seasonality rather than autonomous species interactions.

Similar considerations arise in systems involving competing species, where environmental periodicity may substantially alter the dynamics of the autonomous case, typically balanced between coexistence and competitive exclusion. Namely, for two competing populations with densities u=u⁡(t)u=u(t) and v=v⁡(t)v=v(t), the dynamics of the system

{d​ud​t=μ1​u​(1−u−a1​v),t>0,d​vd​t=μ2​v​(1−v−a2​u),t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{du}{dt}=\mu_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v),&t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\frac{dv}{dt}=\mu_{2}v(1-v-a_{2}u),&t>0,\end{cases} (1)

are well-understood (see for instance [31]), where μ1,μ2>0\mu_{1},\penalty\ \mu_{2}>0 respectively denote the logistic growth rates of species uu and vv, and a1,a2≥0a_{1},\penalty\ a_{2}\geq 0 their interspecific competition coefficients. In particular, if competition is weak, that is, a1,a2∈[0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in[0,1), then the coexistence equilibrium

(u∗,v∗):=(1−a11−a1​a2,1−a21−a1​a2),(u_{*},v_{*})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left(\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}},\frac{1-a_{2}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}\right), (2)

is positive and forms a stable node, which attracts all trajectories with arbitrary positive initial data, while the remaining equilibria, (0,0)(0,0), (1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1) are all unstable. Thus, in this situation, species coexist and their populations densities converge toward the stable equilibrium, without exhibiting sustained oscillatory behavior. If one or both interspecific competition coefficients exceeds 11, a competitive exclusion result is achieved, with one species dominating the other, which eventually becomes extinct.

In contrast, in environments with seasonal variability, the analysis of the following nonautonomous system

{d​ud​t=u⁡(r1​(t)−k1​(t)​u−a1​(t)​v),t>0,d​vd​t=v⁡(r2​(t)−k2​(t)​v−a2​(t)​u),t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{du}{dt}=u\big(r_{1}(t)-k_{1}(t)u-a_{1}(t)v\big),&t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\frac{dv}{dt}=v\big(r_{2}(t)-k_{2}(t)v-a_{2}(t)u\big),&t>0,\end{cases} (3)

reveals substantial qualitative differences, when coefficients ai​(t),ri​(t),ki​(t)a_{i}(t),r_{i}(t),k_{i}(t), i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, are assumed to be continuous, positive and periodic with common period T>0T>0. Under suitable conditions on the coefficients the existence of a unique positive T−T-periodic solution to system (3) can be proved [5], which moreover attracts any other solution with positive initial data. Under such assumptions, regardless of their initial values, both populations converge to a globally attracting positive periodic coexistence state, whose oscillatory behavior is induced by the cyclic environmental conditions. Alternative hypotheses on the coefficients grant the extinction of one of the species, while the other one persists with T−T-periodic oscillations [3, 42].

When spatial dynamics are incorporated into the model, the same distinction between persisting oscillations and convergence to a steady state is preserved when comparing constant environmental conditions with seasonality effects. Namely, let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1 be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then, for the autonomous parabolic system

{∂u∂t=d1​Δ​u+μ1​u​(1−u−a1​v),x∈Ω,t>0,∂v∂t=d2​Δ​v+μ2​v​(1−v−a2​u),x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{1}\Delta u+\mu_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v),&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\Delta v+\mu_{2}v(1-v-a_{2}u),&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases} (4)

with diffusion coefficients d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0, under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, the Lyapunov functional introduced by Goh in [19] for the multiple-species generalization of the ODE system (1) can be easily adapted to the PDE system (4) [4, 24]. As a result, regardless of how fast both species diffuse, their long-time behavior is determined by that of the ODE counterpart. In particular, this implies that for weakly competing species, there is a stable coexistence, with all nontrivial nonnegative solutions converging to the coexistence state (2) uniformly in Ω\Omega. Similarly, competitive exclusion results hold if one of the coefficients ai>1a_{i}>1, leading to the extinction of one of the species [34, 49]. In this way, consistently with the dynamics of the underlying ODE system (1), the autonomous reaction-diffusion system (4) cannot sustain persistent oscillatory dynamics.

In the nonautonomous case, where diffusion is incorporated to system (3), solutions are marked again by oscillatory dynamics, as a result of the seasonality of the environment. In particular, in [2], the authors showed that the sufficient conditions obtained in [5] and in [3] for the ODE system (3) still determine periodic coexistence or competitive exclusion on its diffusive counterpart, independently of the diffusion coefficients. A further attracting property of the periodic orbit in the case of coexistence was determined in [40].

Therefore, seasonality effects in the environmental conditions ultimately induce cyclic oscillations in the populations —both in diffusive and nondiffusive settings— which may arise either through periodic coexistence or through extinction of one species accompanied by periodic persistence of the other. In all these situations, however, the long-time dynamics remain spatially homogeneous and are governed by the balance between the coefficients ai​(t)a_{i}(t), ri​(t)r_{i}(t) and ki​(t)k_{i}(t), i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, which respectively represent the proliferation, self-limitation and competition rates of the species. In particular, for these cases, diffusion preserves the qualitative dynamics of the underlying ODE systems, indicating that spatial spreading alone does not modify the reaction-driven behavior of the species.

This motivates the consideration of further migration mechanisms, to investigate whether the attracting states of the previous systems can be destabilized and give rise to spatially heterogeneous oscillatory structures. In particular, incorporating the effect of chemotaxis, i.e. directed migration in response to a concentration gradient, has revealed very rich dynamics in a broad range of systems (see among others [33, 25, 28]). Moreover, periodicity has been detected in some chemotactically-driven phenomena, such as the movement of Dictyostelium discoideum amoebas toward their center of aggregation [37] or in human neutrophils [14].

Chemotaxis systems with competing species

To study the effect of a self-generated chemoattractant signal on the behavior of two competing species, Tello and Winkler [41] proposed the following Keller–Segel type system,

{∂u∂t=d1Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w)+μ1u(1−u−a1v),x∈Ω,t>0,∂v∂t=d2Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w)+μ2v(1−v−a2u),x∈Ω,t>0,τ​∂w∂t=Δ​w+α​u+β​v−w,x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{1}\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v),&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w)+\mu_{2}v(1-v-a_{2}u),&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\tau\frac{\partial w}{\partial t}=\Delta w+\alpha u+\beta v-w,&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases} (5)

under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions and nonnegative initial data, where u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) again represent the population densities of the two competing species, while w=w⁡(x,t)w=w(x,t) describes the signal concentration. Parameters χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0 respectively denote the chemotactic sensitivity of each species and α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 their self-production rate of the substance. Lastly, τ≥0\tau\geq 0 measures the diffusivity of the signal. For τ=0\tau=0, that is, under a fast diffusion assumption, results in [41, 38] obtained convergence to the corresponding spatially homogeneous steady state under suitable hypotheses in the cases 0≤ai<10\leq a_{i}<1, i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\} leading to coexistence, and for 0≤a2<1<a10\leq a_{2}<1<a_{1} resulting in a competitive exclusion, with uu becoming extinct, and vv proliferating toward its normalized carrying capacity 11. To obtain these results, the logistic growth rates μ1\mu_{1} have to be sufficiently large with respect to the chemotactic sensitivities χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2}, (see also [10] for more refined conditions than those in [41]) ultimately implying that the possible aggregations due to chemotactic effects are effectively overcome by the reaction terms. The work by Bai and Winkler [6] extends these results under similar assumptions to the fully parabolic case, with τ>0\tau>0, while and Negreanu and Vargas [32] considered the nonautonomous setting, similarly yielding convergence of solutions to the underlying ODE reaction dynamics uniformly in space.

In contrast, when the dynamics are not governed by large enough values of the logistic growth rates μi\mu_{i}, different phenomena have been reported to arise. For instance, in absence of kinetic terms, i.e. μ1=μ2=0\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=0, finite-time blow-up of solutions to system (5) has been reported for both τ=0\tau=0 [8, 9, 17] and τ>0\tau>0 [27]. For positive values of μi\mu_{i}, when chemotactic sensitivities are allowed to be sufficiently large, different results have characterized Turing instabilities [47] and the existence of nonconstant steady states [46]. In particular, when crossing a Hopf bifurcation, periodically heterogeneous solutions could be constructed.

The main purpose of this work is to extend these Turing instability results to the nonautonomous case, considering a system of the form

{∂u∂t=d1Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w)+μ1u(1+f1(t)−u−a1v),x∈Ω,t>0,∂v∂t=d2Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w)+μ2v(1+f2(t)−v−a2u),x∈Ω,t>0, 0=Δ​w+α​u+β​v−w,x∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=∂w∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,v(x,0)=v0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{1}\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu_{1}u(1+f_{1}(t)-u-a_{1}v),&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w)+\mu_{2}v(1+f_{2}(t)-v-a_{2}u),&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\penalty\ 0=\Delta w+\alpha u+\beta v-w,&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[7.5347pt] u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0,&x\in\Omega,\end{cases} (6)

as introduced in [32], where ν\nu denotes the outward normal vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Here f1​(t),f2​(t)f_{1}(t),f_{2}(t) are two continuous and bounded TT-periodic functions satisfying

1+fi​(t)>0for all ​t>0,i∈{1,2}.1+f_{i}(t)>0\quad\text{for all }t>0,\penalty\ i\in\{1,2\}. (7)

In this way, at each time t>0t>0, 1+f1​(t)1+f_{1}(t) and 1+f2​(t)1+f_{2}(t) represent the normalized carrying capacity of each species, reflecting the environmental seasonality, which is assumed not to influence neither the logistic growth rates μi\mu_{i} nor the competition rates aia_{i}, which are considered constant. Moreover, without loss of generality, we may assume that after rescaling the variables, d1=d2=1d_{1}=d_{2}=1.

As above mentioned, under suitably small chemotactic sensitivities, namely

μ1>a2​μ2+2​α​(|χ1|+|χ2|),μ2>a1​μ1+2​β​(|χ1|+|χ2|),\mu_{1}>a_{2}\mu_{2}+2\alpha\left(|\chi_{1}|+|\chi_{2}|\right),\quad\mu_{2}>a_{1}\mu_{1}+2\beta\left(|\chi_{1}|+|\chi_{2}|\right), (8)

However, to the best of our knowledge, the effect of high values of χi\chi_{i}, where the state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) could become unstable for system (6), remains unstudied, as well as other scenarios where one or both of the competition rates exceeds 1.

Main results

Throughout this work, we assume that the ODE system (10) possesses a unique nonnegative globally attracting T−T-periodic solution. Since every solution of (10) converges to this periodic orbit, the limit in (9) is independent of the initial values (11). Accordingly, throughout the remainder of the paper we identify (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) with this unique T−T-periodic solution.

With this globally attracting periodic solution to the ODE system (10) as the reference state, our main objective is to characterize its transient linear instability within the full PDE system (6). To this end, we fix all parameters except for χ1\chi_{1}, which we consider as the bifurcation parameter, with the goal of obtaining recurrent unstable dynamics marked by the periodicity of f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}. In particular, we identify time intervals in which (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) becomes linearly unstable, where perturbations are amplified due to the strong taxis effect, followed by stable intervals, where these perturbations decay, and population levels are brought back to (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}). Over time, this mechanism gives rise to recurrent aggregation patterns synchronized with the environmental periodicity.

This contrasts with classical Turing instabilities in autonomous systems, where unstable modes remain permanently unstable once the instability threshold is crossed, or with transient growth phenomena in the autonomous Keller-Segel system with logistic growth in which, if diffusion is small enough, during an intermediate transient phase, population levels can achieve arbitrarily high values, exceeding the environmental carrying capacity, only to decay afterwards, ultimately retaining low densities [48, 26]. In our case, for system (6) transient aggregation phenomena within the interval [0,T][0,T] may become recurrent without the presence of a Hopf bifurcation, driven solely by the environmental periodicity.

The instability conditions are described in the following theorem, which yields a threshold value, denoted χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}} such that for any χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}}, at least one Fourier mode becomes unstable over a certain instability set within [0,T][0,T].

Theorem 1.1.

Assume that f1​(t)f_{1}(t), f2​(t)∈C1​([0,T])f_{2}(t)\in C^{1}([0,T]) are T−T-periodic functions satisfying (7) and that (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) is a nonnegative globally attracting T−T-periodic solution of the ODE system (10) such that

α⁡(1+f2​(t))≤α​a2​u~​(t)+(2​α−a2​β)​v~​(t),for all ​t∈[0,T].\alpha\big(1+f_{2}(t)\big)\leq\alpha a_{2}\tilde{u}(t)+(2\alpha-a_{2}\beta)\tilde{v}(t),\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,T]. (12)

Then, there exists χcrit∈ℝ\chi_{\text{crit}}\in\mathbb{R} such that if χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}}, there is a nonempty set of times ℐ⊂[0,T]\mathcal{I}\subset[0,T] over which the associated spatially homogeneous state (u~,v~,w~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}), where w~:=α​u~+β​v~\tilde{w}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\alpha\tilde{u}+\beta\tilde{v}, is linearly unstable for system (6).

To derive the result, we adapt the method introduced in [44] for nonautonomous reaction–diffusion systems to the cross–diffusive structure of the chemotaxis system (6). This appears to be the first contribution concerning nonautonomous Turing instabilities in chemotaxis–type systems. Theorem 1.1 is complemented by different numerical simulations, in which the value of χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}} is approximated in order to show the destabilizing effect of a large enough χ1\chi_{1} and the subsequent recurrent pattern formation process.

The role of hypothesis (12) in establishing Theorem 1.1 is to provide a solvability criterion for the values of χc(k)\chi_{c}^{(k)} and χ^c(k)\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)}, which are used to define χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}. This becomes clear in the proof of Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3. We remark that assumption (12) is only a sufficient condition, however, it is easy to check numerically once the base state (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) has been computed. A further but more restrictive condition ensuring that (12) is fulfilled can also be derived, based only on the parameter values, as described in Remark 3.1.

Following this introduction, the article is structured as follows. In Section 2, we review some relevant results concerning the ODE system (10), understood within a broader class of periodic competitive systems (3). In particular, sufficient conditions for the existence of a unique globally attracting state are collected in (18) and (19), corresponding to coexistence and competitive exclusion, respectively. These results provide base states (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big), which are globally attracting solutions to the ODE system (10). The linear instability conditions for (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) are then derived in Section 3 through a sequence of auxiliary lemmas, which allow us to to prove Theorem 1.1. Next, Section 4 includes different numerical simulations concerning both cases: first when (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) denotes a periodic coexistence state, and subsequently in a competitive exclusion scenario, where v~​(t)≡0\tilde{v}(t)\equiv 0. Some remarks concerning the location of the instability sets and the case of negative chemotactic sensitivities are gathered in Section 5, and lastly, a discussion of the results obtained and the conclusions are presented in Section 6.

2 Preliminaries: Extinction and periodic coexistence in nonautonomous competitive dynamics

To begin the linear instability analysis of system (6), we first review some known results concerning the dynamics of the associated ODE system (10), not accounting for diffusive and chemotactic effects. System (10) arises as a particular case of the more general class of nonautonomous competitive systems (3), which we reproduce here for convenience

{d​ud​t=u⁡(r1​(t)−k1​(t)​u−a1​(t)​v),t>0,d​vd​t=v⁡(r2​(t)−k2​(t)​v−a2​(t)​u),t>0.\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{du}{dt}=u\big(r_{1}(t)-k_{1}(t)u-a_{1}(t)v\big),&t>0,\\[7.5347pt] \displaystyle\frac{dv}{dt}=v\big(r_{2}(t)-k_{2}(t)v-a_{2}(t)u\big),&t>0.\end{cases} (13)

As mentioned in the Introduction, in contrast to the autonomous setting, time-periodic coefficients may lead to attracting periodic solutions. The first results in this direction are due to de Mottoni and Schiaffino [30]. In particular, by assuming that functions rir_{i}, kik_{i} and aia_{i} are positive, continuous T−T-periodic, for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, they showed that any nonnegative solution to system (13) converges component-wise to another T−T-periodic solution of (13). As a result, the dynamics of the system are asymptotically determined by the three different types of nonnegative T−T-periodic solutions of (13), namely the trivial state (0,0)(0,0); the semitrivial states, of the form (u,0)(u,0) and (0,v)(0,v); and coexistence states, constituted by positive T−T-periodic solutions. Different results have been obtained over the years concerning stability of the different states, as well as existence, multiplicity and attractivity properties of coexistence solutions.

The work of, among others, Ahmad, Álvarez and Lazer in the 1980s and 1990s led to different sufficient conditions for the existence of a unique globally attracting coexistence state, as well as for competitive exclusion behaviors. In particular, by introducing the notation

fM=maxt∈[0,T]⁡f⁡(t),fL=mint∈[0,T]⁡f⁡(t),f^{M}=\max_{t\in[0,T]}f(t),\quad f^{L}=\min_{t\in[0,T]}f(t),

for an arbitrary bounded function ff, the following results were obtained

  1. (i)

    In [5], it was shown that the assumptions

    r1L>a1M​r2Mk2L,r2L>a2M​r1Mk1L,r_{1}^{L}>\frac{a_{1}^{M}r_{2}^{M}}{k_{2}^{L}},\quad r_{2}^{L}>\frac{a_{2}^{M}r_{1}^{M}}{k_{1}^{L}}, (14)

    imply the existence of a unique positive T−T-periodic solution to system (13), (uper​(t),vper​(t))(u^{\text{per}}(t),v^{\text{per}}(t)) which moreover attracts any other solution with positive initial data. In addition, (uper​(t),vper​(t))(u^{\text{per}}(t),v^{\text{per}}(t)) is such that

    r1L​k2L−a1M​r2Mk1M​k2L−a1M​a2L≤uper​(t)≤r1M​k2M−a1L​r2Lk1L​k2M−a1L​a2M,k1L​r2L−r1M​a2Mk1L​k2M−a1L​a2M≤vper​(t)≤k1M​r2M−a2L​r1Lk1M​k2L−a2L​a1M,\begin{split}\frac{r_{1}^{L}k_{2}^{L}-a_{1}^{M}r_{2}^{M}}{k_{1}^{M}k_{2}^{L}-a_{1}^{M}a_{2}^{L}}\leq u^{\text{per}}(t)&\leq\frac{r_{1}^{M}k_{2}^{M}-a_{1}^{L}r_{2}^{L}}{k_{1}^{L}k_{2}^{M}-a_{1}^{L}a_{2}^{M}},\\[6.45831pt] \frac{k_{1}^{L}r_{2}^{L}-r_{1}^{M}a_{2}^{M}}{k_{1}^{L}k_{2}^{M}-a_{1}^{L}a_{2}^{M}}\leq v^{\text{per}}(t)&\leq\frac{k_{1}^{M}r_{2}^{M}-a_{2}^{L}r_{1}^{L}}{k_{1}^{M}k_{2}^{L}-a_{2}^{L}a_{1}^{M}},\end{split} (15)

    This was further extended in [1] to the case of general nonperiodic coefficients, only assuming positivity, continuity and boundedness of rir_{i}, kik_{i} and aia_{i}.

  2. (ii)

    In [3], condition (14) is replaced by

    r1L>a1M​r2Mk2L,r2M≤r1L​a2Lk1M,r_{1}^{L}>\frac{a_{1}^{M}r_{2}^{M}}{k_{2}^{L}},\quad r_{2}^{M}\leq\frac{r_{1}^{L}a_{2}^{L}}{k_{1}^{M}}, (16)

    in which the first inequality coincides with that of (14), while in the second one, maxima and minima are interchanged, as well as the direction of the inequality. Under this assumption, a competitive exclusion is obtained, with the second species eventually becoming extinct, namely

    v⁡(t)→0andu⁡(t)−uper​(t)→0as ​t→∞,v(t)\to 0\quad\text{and}\quad u(t)-u^{\text{per}}(t)\to 0\quad\text{as }t\to\infty, (17)

    where uper​(t)u^{\text{per}}(t) is the unique periodic solution to the decoupled logistic equation

    u′=u⁡(t)​(r1​(t)−k1​(t)​u),t>0.u^{\prime}=u(t)\big(r_{1}(t)-k_{1}(t)u\big),\quad t>0.

    Naturally, a similar result is obtained if the roles of uu and vv are interchanged.

Thus, to guarantee a unique globally attracting periodic coexistence state, conditions (14) require the minimum intrinsic growth rates riLr_{i}^{L} and self-limitation effects kiLk_{i}^{L} of the species to be sufficiently strong, compared to the maximal interspecific competition rates aiMa_{i}^{M}. In contrast, if (14) fails and (16) is satisfied, then the dominant species persists, reaching a periodic regime, while the other one becomes extinct.

With respect to the particular case of system (10), we note that (i) and (ii) read:

  1. 1.

    If

    1+f1L>a1​(1+f2M),1+f2L>a2​(1+f1M),1+f_{1}^{L}>a_{1}\big(1+f_{2}^{M}\big),\quad 1+f_{2}^{L}>a_{2}\big(1+f_{1}^{M}\big), (18)

    then both species coexist periodically. In particular, the system admits a unique positive, periodic and globally attracting coexistence state (uper​(t),vper​(t))\big(u^{\text{per}}(t),v^{\text{per}}(t)\big), to which all other solutions converge to.

  2. 2.

    If

    1+f1L>a1​(1+f2M),1+f2M≤a2​(1+f1L),1+f_{1}^{L}>a_{1}\big(1+f_{2}^{M}\big),\quad 1+f_{2}^{M}\leq a_{2}\big(1+f_{1}^{L}\big), (19)

    then the second species vv becomes extinct, while the first one dominates, and persists with periodic oscillations, converging to uper​(t)u^{\text{per}}(t), the unique periodic solution to

    u′=μ1​u​(1+f1​(t)−u).u^{\prime}=\mu_{1}u\big(1+f_{1}(t)-u\big).

    As a result, this time the orbit (uper​(t),0)\big(u^{\text{per}}(t),0\big) is the only global attractor of the system.

We remark that these are only sufficient conditions, and shall not be interpreted as sharp thresholds. A characterization of the asymptotic stability of the semitrivial states is due to Cushing [13]. In particular, by assuming that

∫0Tr1​(t)​𝑑t>0,∫0Tr2​(t)​𝑑t>0\int_{0}^{T}r_{1}(t)\,dt>0,\quad\int_{0}^{T}r_{2}(t)\,dt>0 (20)

one can define u^\hat{u} and v^\hat{v} as the unique periodic solutions to the uncoupled logistic equations

d​u^d​t=u^​(r1​(t)−k1​(t)​u^),d​v^d​t=v^​(r2​(t)−k2​(t)​v^).\frac{d\hat{u}}{dt}=\hat{u}\big(r_{1}(t)-k_{1}(t)\hat{u}\big),\quad\frac{d\hat{v}}{dt}=\hat{v}\big(r_{2}(t)-k_{2}(t)\hat{v}\big).\\ (21)

Then, by introducing

λ1=1T​∫0T(k1​(t)​u^​(t)−a1​(t)​v^​(t))​𝑑t,λ2=1T​∫0T(k2​(t)​v^​(t)−a2​(t)​u^​(t))​𝑑t\lambda_{1}=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\big(k_{1}(t)\hat{u}(t)-a_{1}(t)\hat{v}(t)\big)\,dt,\quad\lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\big(k_{2}(t)\hat{v}(t)-a_{2}(t)\hat{u}(t)\big)\,dt (22)

one has that the semitrivial state (u^,0)(\hat{u},0) is linearly unstable if and only if λ2>0\lambda_{2}>0, and linearly asymptotically stable if and only if λ2<0\lambda_{2}<0. Similarly, the remaining semitrivial state (0,v^)(0,\hat{v}) is linearly stable if and only if λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 and linearly asymptotically stable if and only if λ1<0\lambda_{1}<0.

If both λ1,λ2>0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0, then both semitrivial states are unstable and the system is persistent. Moreover, this implies that the system admits at least one stable coexistence state (see Eilbeck and López-Gómez [15] for this and for other multiplicity results).

For this work, we only consider states that are global attractors of the ODE system (10), to ensure that instability arises as a result of the spatial effects, and more precisely, of chemotaxis.

3 Linear instability and recurrent aggregation

Having described the sufficient conditions ensuring the existence of a unique nonnegative globally attracting T−T-periodic solution to the ODE system (10) —either corresponding to periodic coexistence or to competitive exclusion—, we now turn to the analysis of its linear stability when regarded as a spatially homogeneous state of the PDE system (6). Following the notation introduced in the Introduction, throughout the remainder of this work, we denote this periodic solution by (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}).

To investigate the linear stability of the spatially homogeneous state (u~,v~,w~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}) for the PDE system (6), where w~​(t):=α​u~​(t)+β​v~​(t)\tilde{w}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\alpha\tilde{u}(t)+\beta\tilde{v}(t), we consider perturbed solutions of the form

u⁡(x,t)=u~​(t)+ε​U​(x,t),v⁡(x,t)=v~​(t)+ε​V​(x,t),w⁡(x,t)=w~​(t)+ε​W​(x,t),u(x,t)=\tilde{u}(t)+\varepsilon U(x,t),\quad v(x,t)=\tilde{v}(t)+\varepsilon V(x,t),\quad w(x,t)=\tilde{w}(t)+\varepsilon W(x,t), (23)

where 0≤ε≪10\leq\varepsilon\ll 1. Substituting solutions (23) into system (6) and neglecting the terms of order ε2\varepsilon^{2} and above, we arrive at the following nonautonomous linearized system for (U,V,W)(U,V,W), given by

{Ut=Δ​U−χ1​u~​(t)​Δ​W+μ1​(1+f1​(t)−2​u~​(t)−a1​v~​(t))​U−μ1​a1​u~​(t)​V,x∈Ω,t>0,Vt=Δ​V−χ2​v~​(t)​Δ​W−μ2​a2​v~​(t)​U+μ2​(1+f2​(t)−2​v~​(t)−a2​u~​(t))​V,x∈Ω,t>0,0=Δ​W+α​U+β​V−W,x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}U_{t}=\Delta U-\chi_{1}\tilde{u}(t)\Delta W+\mu_{1}\big(1+f_{1}(t)-2\tilde{u}(t)-a_{1}\tilde{v}(t)\big)U-\mu_{1}a_{1}\tilde{u}(t)V,&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[6.45831pt] V_{t}=\Delta V-\chi_{2}\tilde{v}(t)\Delta W-\mu_{2}a_{2}\tilde{v}(t)U+\mu_{2}\big(1+f_{2}(t)-2\tilde{v}(t)-a_{2}\tilde{u}(t)\big)V,&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\\[6.45831pt] \hskip 4.26773pt0=\Delta W+\alpha U+\beta V-W,&x\in\Omega,\penalty\ t>0,\end{cases} (24)

together with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions and the respective initial values for UU and VV. By considering the set of eigenvalues {λk}k∈ℕ0\{\lambda_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}} and eigenfunctions {φk}k∈ℕ0\{\varphi_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}} of the operator −Δ-\Delta with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, we can expand (U,V,W)(U,V,W) in Fourier series as follows

U⁡(x,t)=∑k=0∞C1(k)​(t)​φk​(x),V⁡(x,t)=∑k=0∞C2(k)​(t)​φk​(x),W⁡(x,t)=∑k=0∞C3(k)​(t)​φk​(x),U(x,t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}C_{1}^{(k)}(t)\varphi_{k}(x),\quad V(x,t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}C_{2}^{(k)}(t)\varphi_{k}(x),\quad W(x,t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}C_{3}^{(k)}(t)\varphi_{k}(x), (25)

where coefficients (C1(k)​(t),C2(k)​(t),C3(k)​(t))\big(C_{1}^{(k)}(t),C_{2}^{(k)}(t),C_{3}^{(k)}(t)\big) represent the amplitude of the k−k-th spatial mode of the perturbation at time t>0t>0.

The elliptic nature of the third equation allows for further simplification. In particular, by substituting the Fourier expansions (25), and noting that Δ​φk=−λk​φk\Delta\varphi_{k}=-\lambda_{k}\varphi_{k} for each k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, one can solve for coefficients C3(k)​(t)C_{3}^{(k)}(t), yielding

C3(k)​(t)=α​C1(k)​(t)+β​C2(k)​(t)1+λk,t>0.C_{3}^{(k)}(t)=\frac{\alpha C_{1}^{(k)}(t)+\beta C_{2}^{(k)}(t)}{1+\lambda_{k}},\quad t>0. (26)

The main difference with respect to classical autonomous Turing instabilities lies in the time dependence of the matrix Ak​(t)A_{k}(t). In the autonomous setting, the growth of the k−k-th mode is completely determined by the sign of the eigenvalues of a constant matrix. In contrast, the nonconstant structure of (27) prevents such a direct characterization.

While one alternative is to study the Floquet multipliers of AkA_{k} for each k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, that provides a criterion for global instability. Instead, to detect transient instability over subintervals of [0,T][0,T], we analyze the instantaneous growth of C1(k)C_{1}^{(k)} and C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)}. In particular, by differentiation each equation on system (27), it can be converted into a pair of uncoupled second-order linear ODEs of the form

{(C1(k))′′+Pk​(t)​(C1(k))′+Qk​(t)​C1(k)=0,t>0,(C2(k))′′+P^k​(t)​(C2(k))′+Q^k​(t)​C2(k)=0,t>0,\begin{cases}\left(C_{1}^{(k)}\right)^{\prime\prime}+P_{k}(t)\left(C_{1}^{(k)}\right)^{\prime}+Q_{k}(t)\hskip 1.42271ptC_{1}^{(k)}=0,&t>0,\\[8.61108pt] \left(C_{2}^{(k)}\right)^{\prime\prime}+\widehat{P}_{k}(t)\left(C_{2}^{(k)}\right)^{\prime}+\widehat{Q}_{k}(t)\hskip 1.42271ptC_{2}^{(k)}=0,&t>0,\end{cases} (29)

with ′=d/dt{}^{\prime}=d/dt. Naturally, the other semitrivial state (0,v~​(t))\big(0,\tilde{v}(t)\big) follows similarly by exchanging the variables.

In the coexistence case, coefficients PkP_{k}, QkQ_{k}, P^k\widehat{P}_{k} and Q^k\widehat{Q}_{k} in (29) are given by

Pk​(t):=−tr⁡(Ak​(t))−(A12(k)​(t))′A12(k)​(t),\displaystyle P_{k}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=-\tr\big(A_{k}(t)\big)-\frac{\big(A_{12}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}}{A_{12}^{(k)}(t)}, Qk​(t):=det(Ak​(t))−(A11(k)​(t))′+A11(k)​(t)​(A12(k)​(t))′A12(k)​(t),\displaystyle Q_{k}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\det\big(A_{k}(t)\big)-\big(A_{11}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}+A_{11}^{(k)}(t)\frac{\big(A_{12}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}}{A_{12}^{(k)}(t)}, (30)

for all t>0t>0, while for the semitrivial state (u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big), we have A21(k)​(t)≡0A_{21}^{(k)}(t)\equiv 0 for all t>0t>0 and all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}. In particular, the equation for C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)} is uncoupled, and the coefficients are given by

Pk​(t)\displaystyle P_{k}(t) :=−tr(Ak(t))−(A12(k)​(t))′A12(k)​(t),\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=-\tr\big(A_{k}(t)\big)-\frac{\big(A_{12}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}}{A_{12}^{(k)}(t)}, Qk​(t)\displaystyle Q_{k}(t) :=det(Ak(t))−(A11(k)(t))′+A11(k)(t)(A12(k)​(t))′A12(k)​(t),\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\det\big(A_{k}(t)\big)-\big(A_{11}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}+A_{11}^{(k)}(t)\frac{\big(A_{12}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}}{A_{12}^{(k)}(t)}, (31)
P^k​(t)\displaystyle\widehat{P}_{k}(t) :=0,\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=0, Q^k​(t)\displaystyle\widehat{Q}_{k}(t) :=−A22(k)(t).\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=-A_{22}^{(k)}(t).

In both cases, although a complete characterization of the instantaneous growth of C1(k)C_{1}^{(k)} and C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)} may depend on the specific form of the coefficients, a simple sufficient criterion can be found in Theorem A.1 in [44], which we reproduce here for completeness.

Lemma 3.1 (Theorem A.1 in [44]).

Consider linear second-order ODE of the form

y′′+𝒫⁡(t)​y′+𝒬⁡(t)​y=0,t>0,y^{\prime\prime}+\mathcal{P}(t)y^{\prime}+\mathcal{Q}(t)y=0,\quad t>0,

and assume that there exists an interval ℐ⊂[0,∞)\mathcal{I}\subset[0,\infty) such that 𝒬⁡(t)<0\mathcal{Q}(t)<0 for all t∈ℐt\in\mathcal{I}. Then, for any nonzero choice of initial data, the solution y⁡(t)y(t) has an exponential growth rate on ℐ\mathcal{I}.

Thus, from the expressions in (30) and (31), for each fixed t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] we can interpret Qk​(t)Q_{k}(t) and Q^k​(t)\widehat{Q}_{k}(t) as functions of the bifurcation parameter χ1\chi_{1}, which we respectively denote by 𝒬k​(χ1,t)\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t) and 𝒬^k​(χ1,t)\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t). In particular, we first prove that under suitable conditions, the equations

𝒬k​(χ1,t)=0,and𝒬^k​(χ1,t)=0,\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=0,\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=0, (32)

can be uniquely solved with respect to χ1\chi_{1}. This will allow us to identify threshold values associated with the transient amplification of the kk-th perturbation mode. To guarantee the well-posedness of these thresholds, we first establish the following technical lemma concerning the solvability of (32). We begin by the first case, corresponding to the coexistence state, in which 𝒬k​(χ1,t)=0\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=0 and 𝒬^k​(χ1,t)=0\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=0 are as given by the function in (30).

Lemma 3.2.

Let f1​(t)f_{1}(t), f2​(t)∈C1​([0,T])f_{2}(t)\in C^{1}([0,T]) be T−T-periodic functions satisfying (7) and assume that (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) is a positive, globally attracting T−T-periodic coexistence state of system (10) such that (12) holds. Then for each k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, there exist continuous functions ak,bk,b^k:[0,T]→ℝa_{k},b_{k},\widehat{b}_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} such that

with the property that ak​(t)<0a_{k}(t)<0 for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. For a fixed k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+} we first prove that for each t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], the maps χ1↦𝒬k​(χ1,t)\chi_{1}\mapsto\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t) and χ1↦𝒬^k​(χ1,t)\chi_{1}\mapsto\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t) are affine. Indeed, we recall that from (30) one has

Qk​(t)=det(Ak​(t))−(A11(k)​(t))′+A11(k)​(t)​(A12(k)​(t))′A12(k)​(t),Q^k​(t)=det(Ak​(t))−(A22(k)​(t))′+A22(k)​(t)​(A21(k)​(t))′A21(k)​(t),\begin{split}Q_{k}(t)=\det\big(A_{k}(t)\big)-\big(A_{11}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}+A_{11}^{(k)}(t)\frac{\big(A_{12}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}}{A_{12}^{(k)}(t)},\\[6.45831pt] \widehat{Q}_{k}(t)=\det\big(A_{k}(t)\big)-\big(A_{22}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}+A_{22}^{(k)}(t)\frac{\big(A_{21}^{(k)}(t)\big)^{\prime}}{A_{21}^{(k)}(t)},\end{split}

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], where

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. As a result, (33) holds, that is, for each fixed t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], there exist three continuous functions ak,bk,b^k:[0,T]→ℝa_{k},b_{k},\widehat{b}_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} such that

ak​(t)=u~​(t)​α​λk1+λk​(−λk+μ2​[1+f2​(t)−a2​u~​(t)−(2−a2​βα)​v~​(t)]),for all ​t∈[0,T].a_{k}(t)=\tilde{u}(t)\frac{\alpha\lambda_{k}}{1+\lambda_{k}}\left(-\lambda_{k}+\mu_{2}\left[1+f_{2}(t)-a_{2}\tilde{u}(t)-\left(2-\frac{a_{2}\beta}{\alpha}\right)\tilde{v}(t)\right]\right),\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,T]. completing the proof. ∎

Next, we prove a similar result for the semitrivial state (u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big). This time, however, we shall see that the cancellations in the second equation result in only being able to define χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)}, as for the second equation one always has 𝒬^k​(χ1,t)>0\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)>0 for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+} and all t>0t>0, χ1∈ℝ\chi_{1}\in\mathbb{R}.

Lemma 3.3.

Assume that functions f1​(t)f_{1}(t), f2​(t)∈C1​([0,T])f_{2}(t)\in C^{1}([0,T]) are T−T-periodic and that they fulfill (7). Suppose moreover that (u~​(t),v~​(t))=(u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big)=\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big) is a T−T-periodic globally attracting semitrivial state of system (10) such that the corresponding version of (12) is satisfied. Then, for each k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, there exist continuous functions ak,bk:[0,T]→ℝa_{k},b_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} such that

𝒬k​(χ1,t)=ak​(t)​χ1+bk​(t),\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=a_{k}(t)\chi_{1}+b_{k}(t), (37)

with ak​(t)<0a_{k}(t)<0 for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. As a result, for each t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], the equation 𝒬k​(χ1,t)=0\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=0 has a unique solution in χ1\chi_{1}, denoted by χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t). Moreover, 𝒬^k​(χ1,t)>0\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)>0 for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, all t>0t>0 and all χ1∈ℝ\chi_{1}\in\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

The only difference with respect to the previous coexistence case lies on the second equation, as now A21(k)​(t)≡0A_{21}^{(k)}(t)\equiv 0 for all t>0t>0 and all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}. Consequently, according to (31), C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)} now satisfies the second-order equation

(C2(k))′′−A22(k)​(t)​C2(k)=0,t>0.\Big(C_{2}^{(k)}\Big)^{\prime\prime}-A_{22}^{(k)}(t)\,C_{2}^{(k)}=0,\quad t>0.

In particular, as v~​(t)≡0\tilde{v}(t)\equiv 0, the expression for A22(k)​(t)A_{22}^{(k)}(t) in (28) now simplifies to

A22(k)​(t)=−λk+μ2​(1+f2​(t)−a2​u~​(t)),for all ​t>0.A_{22}^{(k)}(t)=\displaystyle-\lambda_{k}+\mu_{2}\big(1+f_{2}(t)-a_{2}\tilde{u}(t)\big),\quad\text{for all }t>0.

Moreover, by hypothesis (12), again since v~​(t)≡0\tilde{v}(t)\equiv 0, we have that

1+f2​(t)≤a2​u~​(t),for all ​t>0,1+f_{2}(t)\leq a_{2}\tilde{u}(t),\quad\text{for all }t>0,

which directly implies that A22(k)​(t)<0A_{22}^{(k)}(t)<0. As a result, we have that for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+} and for any choice of χ1∈ℝ\chi_{1}\in\mathbb{R}

𝒬^k​(χ1,t)=−A22(k)​(t)>0,for all ​t>0.\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=-A_{22}^{(k)}(t)>0,\quad\text{for all }t>0.

For 𝒬k​(χ1,t)\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t), as A12(k)​(t)A_{12}^{(k)}(t) does not in general vanish, the result follows from the same steps as in the proof of Lemma 3.2. ∎

As a result of Lemma 3.3, in the case of a semitrivial state of the form (u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big), the transient instability condition from Lemma 3.1 can never be satisfied by the modal amplitudes C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)}, k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}. Hence, no instability of these modes can be detected by means of this criterion. We remark however that since Lemma 3.1 is only a sufficient condition for exponential growth, this does not imply that the corresponding perturbations are stable or decay to zero.

Remark 3.1.

We emphasize again that condition (7) is not implicit, and can be numerically checked with the selected values of α,β,a2>0\alpha,\beta,a_{2}>0 once the base state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) has been computed. Moreover, using the bounds in (15), a further sufficient condition can be derived involving only the parameters of the system, without requiring explicit knowledge of (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}). Nevertheless, it is generally more restrictive, as it replaces the pointwise verification of (12) by a global estimate.

Guaranteeing the solvability of equations (32), or for the first of them in the case of a semitrivial state, allows us to define thresholds values for χ1\chi_{1}, which characterize the growth of at least one Fourier mode of the perturbations throughout a certain subinterval of [0,T][0,T]. As previously, we begin by the case in which (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) represents a positive coexistence state.

Lemma 3.4.

Let f1​(t)f_{1}(t), f2​(t)∈C1​([0,T])f_{2}(t)\in C^{1}([0,T]) be T−T-periodic functions satisfying (7) and assume that (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) is a positive T−T-periodic globally attracting coexistence state of system (10) such that (12) holds. Then, for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, there exists a value χc(k)∈ℝ\chi_{c}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R} such that if χ1>χc(k)\chi_{1}>\chi_{c}^{(k)}, the first component C1(k)C_{1}^{(k)} of the solution to system (27) has an exponential growth rate over a set of times Ik⊂[0,T]I_{k}\subset[0,T].

Proof.

For a given k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, we consider the equivalent formulation of system (27) given in (29). We seek to apply Lemma 3.1, using the properties of 𝒬k\mathcal{Q}_{k} proved in Lemma 3.2. In particular, we define the threshold

χc(k):=inft∈[0,T]χ1(k)​(t),\chi_{c}^{(k)}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\inf_{t\in[0,T]}\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t), (38)

where we recall for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) denotes the unique solution to the equation 𝒬k​(χ1,t)=0\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=0. Since 𝒬k​(χ1,t)=ak​(t)​χ1+bk​(t)\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=a_{k}(t)\chi_{1}+b_{k}(t), with ak​(t)<0a_{k}(t)<0 over [0,T][0,T], then for any t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]

𝒬k​(χ1,t)​<0if and only ifχ1>​χ1(k)​(t).\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)<0\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\chi_{1}>\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t).

As a result, for any χ1>χc(k)\chi_{1}>\chi_{c}^{(k)}, there exists at least one time t0∈[0,T]t_{0}\in[0,T] such that χ1>χ1(k)​(t0)\chi_{1}>\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t_{0}), and thus 𝒬k​(χ1,t0)<0\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t_{0})<0. Moreover, due to the continuity of 𝒬k​(χ1,⋅)\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},\cdot) on [0,T][0,T] asserted by Lemma 3.2, there exists at least one interval Ik⊂[0,T]I_{k}\subset[0,T] containing t0t_{0} such that 𝒬k​(χ1,t)<0\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)<0, for all t∈Ikt\in I_{k}. Hence, by Lemma 3.1, the first component C1(k)C_{1}^{(k)} exhibits an exponential growth rate on IkI_{k}. ∎

Remark 3.2.

For a given χ1>χc(k)\chi_{1}>\chi_{c}^{(k)}, the set of instability times associated with the kk-th mode,

Ik=Ik(χ1):={t∈[0,T]:𝒬k(χ1,t)<0},I_{k}=I_{k}(\chi_{1})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\{\,t\in[0,T]\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathcal{Q}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)<0\,\},

is, in general, not a single interval. In general, it depends on the value of χ1\chi_{1} and of the function χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t).

A counterpart to Lemma 3.4 with respect to the C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)} equation can be similarly proved in the same way. We omit the details of the proof, as it follows the same steps, based on second-order formulation (29) and the solvability of 𝒬^k​(χ1,t)=0\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)=0 for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] granted by Lemma 3.2.

Lemma 3.5.

Suppose that f1​(t)f_{1}(t), f2​(t)∈C1​([0,T])f_{2}(t)\in C^{1}([0,T]) are T−T-periodic functions fulfilling (7) and that (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) is a positive T−T-periodic globally attracting coexistence state of system (10) satisfying assumption (12). Then, for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, there exists χ^c(k)∈ℝ\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)}\in\mathbb{R} such that if χ1>χ^c(k)\chi_{1}>\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)}, the second component C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)} of the solution to system (27) has an exponential growth rate over a set of times I^k⊂[0,T]\widehat{I}_{k}\subset[0,T].

As in Lemma 3.4, for each k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, χ^c(k)\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)} is defined as

χ^c(k):=inft∈[0,T]χ^1(k)​(t).\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\inf_{t\in[0,T]}\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\,(k)}(t). (39)

We also emphasize that as described in Remark 3.2, in general for a given k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+} and χ1>χ^c(k)\chi_{1}>\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)} the set of instability times I^k\widehat{I}_{k} for C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)} need not be a single interval.

Lastly, for the semitrivial state (u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big), as a consequence of Lemma 3.3, only a similar result to Lemma 3.4 can be proved, ruling out any instability arising from the growth of C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)}. Again, we omit the details of the proof, as it follows the same structure.

Lemma 3.6.

Assume f1​(t)f_{1}(t), f2​(t)∈C1​([0,T])f_{2}(t)\in C^{1}([0,T]) are T−T-periodic functions satisfying (7) and that (u~​(t),v~​(t))=(u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big)=\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big) is a globally attracting T−T-periodic semitrivial state of system (10) verifying (12). Then, for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, there exists a value χc(k)∈ℝ\chi_{c}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R} such that if χ1>χc(k)\chi_{1}>\chi_{c}^{(k)}, the first component C1(k)C_{1}^{(k)} of the solution to system (27) has an exponential growth rate over a set of times Ik⊂[0,T]I_{k}\subset[0,T].

The proof of Theorem 1.1 now becomes an immediate consequence of Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5 in the case of positive coexistence, and of Lemma 3.6 for the semitrivial state.

Proof of Theorem 1.1
  We first consider the case in which (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) represents a coexistence state. Then, defining χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}} as

χcrit:=infk∈ℕ+{χc(k),χ^c(k)},\chi_{\text{crit}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}\left\{\chi_{c}^{(k)},\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)}\right\}, (40)

where, for each k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, χc(k)\chi_{c}^{(k)} and χ^c(k)\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)} are as respectively defined in Lemma (38) and (39). Then, for any χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}}, we introduce

𝒦1:={k∈ℕ+,χ1>χc(k)},𝒦2:={k∈ℕ+,χ1>χ^c(k)}.\mathcal{K}_{1}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left\{\,k\in\mathbb{N}^{+},\penalty\ \chi_{1}>\chi_{c}^{(k)}\,\right\},\quad\mathcal{K}_{2}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left\{\,k\in\mathbb{N}^{+},\penalty\ \chi_{1}>\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)}\,\right\}.

In this way, 𝒦:=𝒦1∪𝒦2\mathcal{K}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathcal{K}_{1}\cup\mathcal{K}_{2}, which is clearly nonempty by definition of χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}, is the set of unstable modes. As a result, by considering the instability time sets

ℐ1:=⋃k∈𝒦1Ik,ℐ2:=⋃k∈𝒦2I^k,\mathcal{I}_{1}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\bigcup_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{1}}I_{k},\quad\mathcal{I}_{2}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\bigcup_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{2}}\widehat{I}_{k}, (41)

we may define

ℐ:=ℐ1∪ℐ2.\mathcal{I}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\mathcal{I}_{2}. (42)

Consequently, by construction of ℐ\mathcal{I}, for all t∈ℐt\in\mathcal{I}, there exists at least one mode k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K} such that the k−k-th modal amplitude (C1(k)​(t),C2(k)​(t))\big(C_{1}^{(k)}(t),C_{2}^{(k)}(t)\big) has an exponential growth rate at time tt in at least one of its components. This implies the transient linear instability of the state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) over ℐ\mathcal{I}.

For the case of a semitrivial state, if (u~​(t),v~​(t))=(u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big)=\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big), then the threshold χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}} can be similarly defined, taking into account that by Lemma 3.3, 𝒬^k​(χ1,t)>0\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)>0 for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, all t>0t>0 and all χ1∈ℝ\chi_{1}\in\mathbb{R}. Thus, the only instability that can be characterized by Lemma 3.1 comes from χc(k)\chi_{c}^{(k)}, and consequently we define

χcrit:=infk∈ℕ+{χc(k)}.\chi_{\text{crit}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}\left\{\chi_{c}^{(k)}\right\}. (43)

All the previous steps can be reproduced here, but only for the growth of the modes C1(k)C_{1}^{(k)}, as in this case 𝒦=𝒦1\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_{1} and ℐ=ℐ1\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}_{1}. ∎

Remark 3.3.

The significance of Theorem 1.1 lies in the fact that the instability mechanism is intrinsically linked to the temporal periodicity of the spatially homogeneous state. Indeed, if χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}}, then there exists a nonempty set of times ℐ⊂[0,T]\mathcal{I}\subset[0,T] on which at least one spatial mode exhibits exponential growth. Since all coefficients in the linearized problem are T−T-periodic, the same instability mechanism reappears during every subsequent period. Consequently, the state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) is linearly unstable over each translated set of times

ℐ+kT:={t+kT:t∈ℐ},k∈ℕ0\mathcal{I}+kT\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\left\{t+kT\penalty\ \mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\penalty\ t\in\mathcal{I}\right\},\quad k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}

In this sense, Theorem 1.1 establishes the existence of a recurrent sequence of transient instability time sets generated by the external periodicity of functions f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}.

4 Numerical examples

After establishing the proof of Theorem 1.1 in the previous section, we now present different numerical simulations aimed at identifying the threshold value χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}} and its associated instability time set. This allows us to explore the periodic arising of different spatial patterns that are generated by the dynamics of system (6). We consider both cases for the spatially homogeneous state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}), periodic coexistence, where both components are positive, and competitive exclusion, corresponding to a semitrivial state.

4.1 Periodic coexistence

We begin by considering the case in which the ODE system (10) admits a unique, positive, globally attracting, periodic coexistence state, (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big). To ensure its existence and uniqueness, we assume that aia_{i} and fif_{i} are such that (18) holds.

We analyze two different examples. In the first, the functions fif_{i}, representing the time variation of the carrying capacities, are in phase, attaining their maxima and minima simultaneously. In the second, we consider out-of-phase dynamics, so that the most favorable environmental conditions for one species coincide with the least favorable conditions for the other.

4.1.1 Example I: In-phase carrying capacities

To begin the first example with synchronized carrying capacities, we consider a large enough one-dimensional domain, given by Ω=(0,50)\Omega=(0,50), and the following parameters

a1=0.25,a2=0.2,μ1=1,μ2=2.5,α=1,β=0.8,χ2=1.5,1+f1(t)=1−0.6sin(0.25t),1+f2(t)=1−0.5sin(0.25t).\begin{gathered}a_{1}=0.25,\quad a_{2}=0.2,\quad\mu_{1}=1,\quad\mu_{2}=2.5,\quad\alpha=1,\quad\beta=0.8,\\[6.45831pt] \chi_{2}=1.5,\quad 1+f_{1}(t)=1-0.6\sin(0.25t),\quad 1+f_{2}(t)=1-0.5\sin(0.25t)\,.\end{gathered} (44)

Parameters (44) represent for instance two different competing phenotypes of a bacterial species. Phenotype I, corresponding to the first species uu presents a slower reproduction rate μ1\mu_{1} than Phenotype II, which can proliferate faster. Both have relatively similar (weak) competition coefficients a1a_{1}, a2a_{2}, and self-production rates of the chemoattractant α\alpha and β\beta. The environmental conditions, encoded by the time-dependent carrying capacities 1+fi1+f_{i} are synchronized, and affect both phenotypes in a similar way, with a period of T=8​πT=8\pi. Phenotype I is however slightly more responsive to environmental changes, attaining its maximum carrying capacity of 1+0.61+0.6 at times t=6​π+k​Tt=6\pi+kT, k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0} and minimum 0.40.4 at t=2​π+k​Tt=2\pi+kT, k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, compared to phenotype II, whose carrying capacity oscillates between 0.5 and 1.5. Phenotype II presents a moderate chemotactic sensitivity, with a coefficient χ2=1.5\chi_{2}=1.5, and we recall that the diffusion coefficient of both phenotypes is normalized to 1.

Our aim is thus to determine the critical chemotactic sensitivity coefficient of the first phenotype that leads to the instability of the periodic coexistence state (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big). To do so, we first verify that conditions (18) are satisfied by our choice of aia_{i} and fif_{i}, in order to ensure that such a unique coexistence state exists and that it is globally attracting. In particular, it is direct to check that

1+f1L=0.4>0.25⋅1.5=a1​(1+f2M)and1+f2L=0.5>0.2⋅1.6=a2​(1+f1M).1+f_{1}^{L}=0.4>0.25\cdot 1.5=a_{1}\big(1+f_{2}^{M}\big)\quad\text{and}\quad 1+f_{2}^{L}=0.5>0.2\cdot 1.6=a_{2}\big(1+f_{1}^{M}\big).

Moreover, we numerically verify that hypothesis (12) holds, to grant the solvability of equations (32), leading to the thresholds χc(k)\chi_{c}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\penalty\ (k)} for each mode. To approximate the state (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big), which is the unique global attractor of system (10), we choose arbitrary initial data and numerically integrate the system over successive periods. We then evaluate the solution at times tk=k​Tt_{k}=kT, k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, until the difference between two consecutive evaluations falls below a prescribed tolerance. This provides us an approximation of initial value (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) that generates the periodic coexistence state (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big).

Computing (u~​(t),v~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)\big) in this way, we verify that (12) holds, as depicted in Figure 1. In particular, we find that the red curve, corresponding to α​(1+f2​(t))\alpha\big(1+f_{2}(t)\big) lies below the blue curve, α​a2​u~​(t)+(2​α−a2​β)​v~​(t)\alpha a_{2}\tilde{u}(t)+\big(2\alpha-a_{2}\beta\big)\tilde{v}(t), for all times.

Specifically, we discretize the interval [0,T]=[0,8​π][0,T]=[0,8\pi] by considering 500 evenly spaced nodes, over which we solve both linear equations (32). This is done for all modes k∈{1,…,30}k\in\{1,\dots,30\}, and the resulting functions are plotted in Figure 2. The leading modes require very large values of χ1\chi_{1} to be destabilized. In particular, both χ1(1)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(1)}(t) and χ^1(1)​(t)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\penalty\ (1)}(t) lie above 200200 for the majority of [0,T][0,T], while the corresponding values for k=2k=2 they are of order 100100. As kk increases, the magnitude of χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) and χ^1(k)​(t)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\penalty\ (k)}(t), decreases rapidly at first, and then begins to stabilize for intermediate vales of kk. To better illustrate this growth in the magnitude of χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) and χ^1(k)​(t)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\penalty\ (k)}(t) with respect to kk, Figure 3 depicts the quantities

χc(k):=inft∈[0,T]χ1(k)(t),χ^c(k):=inft∈[0,T]χ^1(k)(t),\chi_{c}^{(k)}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\inf_{t\in[0,T]}\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t),\quad\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\,(k)}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\inf_{t\in[0,T]}\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\penalty\ (k)}(t),

χcrit=infk∈ℕ+{χc(k),χ^c(k)}=χ^c(18)≈3.287,\chi_{\text{crit}}=\inf_{k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}\left\{\chi_{c}^{(k)},\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (k)}\right\}=\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\penalty\ (18)}\approx 3.287,

Hence, the first modal amplitude to become linearly unstable is C2(18)C_{2}^{(18)}, corresponding to the eighteenth spatial mode of vv.

Referring back to Figure 2, we represent the value of χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}} in gray dashed lines on the center and right panels. As it can be seen, the minimum is precisely attained in the bottom right panel, for the mode k=18k=18, shortly before t=20t=20. As χc(18)\chi_{c}^{(18)} is also very close to the infimum, a similar behavior is found on the top right panel for χ1(18)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(18)}(t). Consequently, Theorem 1.1 implies that, for any χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}}, there exists an instability time set ℐ⊂[0,T]\mathcal{I}\subset[0,T] and a collection of modes 𝒦\mathcal{K} over which the periodic coexistence state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) becomes linearly unstable.

In the previous phenotypical interpretation of the model, the value χcrit≈3.287\chi_{\text{crit}}\approx 3.287 represents the minimum chemotactic sensitivity required for Phenotype I to destabilize the homogeneous coexistence state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}). Since this threshold is more than twice the value of the chemotactic sensitivity of Phenotype II (χ2=1.5\chi_{2}=1.5), instability occurs only when Phenotype I exhibits a substantially stronger tendency to move along chemoattractant gradients. The instability mechanism can therefore be interpreted as arising from the interaction between a highly chemotactic-responsive but moderately reproducing phenotype, and a less motile phenotype with a higher reproduction rate. Consequently, if the chemotaxis sensitivity of Phenotype I is above χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}, Theorem 1.1 predicts the emergence of transient bacterial aggregations during specific portions of each environmental cycle, which reappear on each subsequent cycle due to the environmental periodicity.

With the aim of verifying this behavior numerically by computing the solution to system (6), we take for instance χ1=6>χcrit\chi_{1}=6>\chi_{\text{crit}}. For reference, this value is indicated by the black dashed line in the central and right panels of Figure 2. The corresponding instability set ℐ⊂[0,T]\mathcal{I}\subset[0,T] can then be identified directly from the graphs of χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\penalty\ (k)}, consisting of all times for which at least one of these curves lies below the level χ1=6\chi_{1}=6. In particular, we numerically obtain that

ℐ=[0,t1)∪(t2,T]≈[0,3.412)∪(9.219,25.132].\mathcal{I}=[0,t_{1})\cup(t_{2},T]\approx[0,3.412)\cup(9.219,25.132]. (45)

Therefore, Theorem 1.1 predicts the arise of a transient instability during the initial and final portions of each environmental cycle. Moreover, as stated in Remark 3.3, the instability set is translated over each environmental cycle, and since the interval (t2,T](t_{2},T] from the first period is followed by the interval [T,t1+T)[T,t_{1}+T), we find that for the complete evolution problem over [0,∞)[0,\infty), the coexistence state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) is linearly unstable over the set

ℐ∞:=[0,t1)∪(t2,t1+T)∪(t2+T,t1+2​T)∪(t2+2​T,t1+3​T)∪…\mathcal{I}_{\infty}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=[0,t_{1})\cup(t_{2},t_{1}+T)\cup(t_{2}+T,t_{1}+2T)\cup(t_{2}+2T,t_{1}+3T)\cup\dots (46)
