In addition to ℐ\mathcal{I}, we also approximate the sets ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} and ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} defined in (41), which collect the times at which at least one modal amplitude C1(k)C_{1}^{(k)} or C2(k)C_{2}^{(k)}, respectively, has an exponential growth rate. Therefore ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} and ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} respectively characterize the sets of transient instability of uu and vv. A numerical approximation yields

ℐ1=[0,3.283)∪(9.219,25.132],ℐ2=[0,3.412)∪(9.219,25.132].\mathcal{I}_{1}=[0,3.283)\cup(9.219,25.132],\quad\mathcal{I}_{2}=[0,3.412)\cup(9.219,25.132]. (47)

As we see, given the high similarity of χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) and χ^1(k)​(t)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\penalty\ (k)}(t), both instability sets ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} and ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} are very similar, and in fact their second half coincides. However, uu may loose instability at t=3.283t=3.283, just shortly before vv, at t=3.412t=3.412. With the aim of extending the analysis over more than one environmental cycle, in the same way that ℐ∞\mathcal{I}_{\infty} was defined in (46), we consider the corresponding analogous ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)} for ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} and ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2}, respectively.

To investigate the relationship between the environmental conditions and the transient source of instability, Figure 4 shows the carrying capacities 1+f11+f_{1} and 1+f21+f_{2} and the periodic coexistence states (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}), aside the instability sets ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)}, represented in red over the time axis. The complement sets [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(1)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(2)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)} —the only time sets in which linear stability may hold— are represented in green. Here and below, we refer to the complement sets [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(i)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(i)} as non-instability sets. This should not be interpreted as implying stability on [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(i)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(i)}, rather, it only indicates that the instability criterion provided by Lemma 3.1 does not detect exponential growth over them. Nevertheless, any intervals on which linear stability may occur must necessarily be contained in these non-instability sets.

The results seem to indicate how the instability sets ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)} occur in phases where the respective carrying capacities 1+f11+f_{1} and 1+f21+f_{2} attain sufficiently large values, while on the contrary, the only possible stability sets, [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(1)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(2)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)} are observed only near their minima. This could suggest that instability is only detected when the environmental conditions are sufficiently favorable for growth, and consequently the populations are not strongly constrained by low carrying capacities. However, as we shall see in Example II and in more detail in Section 5, this is not generally true, and there is a particular balance that governs the location of the instability sets, rather than directly coinciding with high-enough carrying capacities.

After the analytical characterization of the transient stability provided by the sets ℐ\mathcal{I}, ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} and ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2}, we next turn to the simulation of the complete system (6) in order to observe wether such instability can give rise to recurrent spatial patterns. In particular, a second-order finite-difference scheme is used, with constant grid spacing Δ​x=0.05\Delta x=0.05 and time step Δ​t=2⋅10−3\Delta t=2\cdot 10^{-3}. As initial data, we take a small perturbation of (u~​(0),v~​(0))\big(\tilde{u}(0),\tilde{v}(0)\big), given for instance by

u⁡(x,0)=u~​(0)+ε​sin⁡(π​x/50),v⁡(x,0)=v~​(0)+ε​cos⁡(π​x/50),u(x,0)=\tilde{u}(0)+\varepsilon\sin(\pi x/50),\quad v(x,0)=\tilde{v}(0)+\varepsilon\cos(\pi x/50), (48)

for ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05. This allows us to compare the obtained solution with the periodic coexistence state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}), which is globally attracting for the non-diffusive and non-chemotactic system (10). The results are depicted in Figure 5, with the left panel showing the comparison u−u~u-\tilde{u}, the center panel portraying v−v~v-\tilde{v}, and the right panel w−w~w-\tilde{w}, where we recall that w~​(t):=α​u~​(t)+β​v~​(t)\tilde{w}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\alpha\tilde{u}(t)+\beta\tilde{v}(t).

As it can be observed on the three panels, after an initial period during which the solution remains close to the spatially homogeneous state, lasting until shortly before t=20t=20, the three components uu, vv and ww develop highly structured spatial patterns. For uu and vv, these take the form of nine symmetric population aggregates (plus two, one on each side of the boundary) that rise above the equilibrium levels u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v}, concentrating the majority of the population. In the case of uu, the larger chemotaxis sensitivity (χ1=6>1.5=χ2\chi_{1}=6>1.5=\chi_{2}) leads to significantly stronger aggregations than those observed for vv, with the maximum deviation from u~\tilde{u} exceeding 22, while the maximum difference between vv and v~\tilde{v} is one order below, at 0.250.25. With respect to ww, the highest concentrations of the chemoattractant occur precisely in the regions where the population clusters are located, reflecting the combined effects of chemotactic attraction and self-production.

This instability period, spanning approximately from t=20t=20 to t=30t=30, is next followed by a second stable regime, where spatial heterogeneities decay and the solution returns close to the homogeneous periodic state (u~,v~,w~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}). At approximately t=40t=40, spatial heterogeneities begin to reappear, giving rise to a new phase of pattern formation, somewhat longer than the first one. This alternation between stable and unstable periods, with recurrent intervals of strong aggregation, is observed until the end of the simulation, after four environmental cycles. Only the first unstable period is observed to be shorter than the other ones, of approximately equal length.

To better analyze the effect of the instability sets ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)} and their complements in the emergence of spatial heterogeneities, the left panel of Figure 6 represents the temporal evolution of maxx∈Ω⁡u⁡(x,t)\max_{x\in\Omega}u(x,t) and maxx∈Ω⁡v⁡(x,t)\max_{x\in\Omega}v(x,t), aside the periodic coexistence state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}), in dotted yellow line. The instability sets ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)} are also represented on the time axis in red, as well as their complements, in green.

During the initial instants of the simulation, although both components lie within their respective instability sets, spatial heterogeneity is minimal, with both maximum plots presenting no deviations from the state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}). This is followed by a first non-instability period, represented in green, which extends approximately until t=10t=10 (both intervals ending precisely at 9.2199.219, as computed in (47)), where both solutions still remain close to the spatially homogeneous state. It is during the second instability period, when spatial heterogeneity starts to develop. Due to the strong taxis effect, as previously discussed, the destabilizing effect is greater for uu, resulting in patterns that reach a maximum population density above 3.53.5, approximately at t=19.5t=19.5. In contrast, the deviations of vv remain substantially scarcer, with its maximum density reaching only about 1.51.5.

To further analyze the shape of the emerging patterns, the spatial profiles of uu, vv and ww are represented on the right panel of Figure 6. The first plot corresponds precisely to t=19.5t=19.5, the time at which the largest deviations of uu from u~\tilde{u} were observed. As shown by the blue curve, several symmetric spike-like aggregates emerge, with the largest population densities nearly reaching 44, close to x=15x=15 and x=35x=35. The corresponding profiles of vv and ww, respectively represented in red and yellow, show substantially less spatial variation, especially in the case of vv. The self-production of the chemoattractant by the two species results in similar high concentrations of ww located at the maxima of uu, although significantly damped due to the comparatively homogeneous distribution of vv.

After some time, as the periods of instability reach an end, the previously formed aggregates begin to dissipate and the maximum values gradually decrease, returning towards the spatially homogeneous profile (u~​(t),v~​(t))(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t)), as illustrated again in the left panel of Figure 6. During this subsequent stable regime, as already inferred from the plots in Figure 5, spatial heterogeneities decay. This is further confirmed by the spatial profiles at t=33t=33 (second plot on the right panel), where only small oscillations remain, negligible compared to the structures observed at t=19.5t=19.5.

This alternation between growth and decay persists over the subsequent environmental cycles: instability phases generate pattern formation within the sets ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)}, while stability phases, corresponding to their complements, drive the solution back toward (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}).

One important dynamical feature is observed during the first environmental cycle. As previously noted, the first pattern formation process is slightly delayed with respect to the others, not reaching an aggregation stage until nearly t=20t=20, resulting in a longer initial stable stage, as opposed to the subsequent ones. This is most likely due to the fact that the first instability intervals are relatively short, ending at t≈3.283t\approx 3.283 for uu and t≈3.412t\approx 3.412 for vv, and are followed by a prolonged non-instability phase, spanning until t≈9.219t\approx 9.219 in both cases. Combined with small initial perturbations, this prevents the early amplification of spatial heterogeneities, which only begin to develop near t=20t=20. As a result, the patterns that emerge on the first environmental cycle differ from those observed in later cycles.

This effect is visible in both panels on Figure 6. On the left-hand side, the first significant deviation from (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) occurs approximately after t=18t=18 and its shape is not reproduced in subsequent cycles, which instead display more regular characteristics. This is also noticeable in the spatial profiles, on the right panel. In particular, the profiles at t=19.5+T≈44.633t=19.5+T\approx 44.633 are more evenly distributed than those at t=19.5t=19.5, and exhibit a reduced maximal amplitude, remaining below 33, with the peak occurring earlier at approximately t≈41.82t\approx 41.82, as visible on the left panel.

To investigate the abrupt changes observed in the graph of max⁡u⁡(⋅,t)\max u(\cdot,t) in Figure 6 during the first growth phase, we represent additional spatial profiles of uu near t=20t=20 in the top row of Figure 7. Rapid changes in the bacterial density are observed, especially in the central region of the domain. In particular, after the profile at t=19.5t=19.5, previously shown in Figure 6, the two central aggregates merge into a single cluster by t=20t=20. At this stage, the maximum density has fallen, and is now close to 33. Shortly afterwards, at t=20.2t=20.2, the two neighboring aggregates experience a rapid increase in density, before partially dissipating again by t=20.75t=20.75, due to the increase in the central cluster. These local reorganizations explain the non-smooth behavior observed in the evolution of max⁡u⁡(⋅,t)\max u(\cdot,t) during this interval.

To further analyze the recurrent dynamics observed in later environmental cycles, the bottom row of Figure 7 shows the spatial profiles of uu at t=41.8t=41.8, corresponding to the largest value attained by max⁡u⁡(⋅,t)\max u(\cdot,t) during the second cycle, and at t=50.5t=50.5, during the subsequent decay phase, together with the corresponding profiles one period later, namely at t=41.8+T≈66.933t=41.8+T\approx 66.933 and t=50.5+T≈75.632t=50.5+T\approx 75.632. The profiles obtained in both cycles are remarkably similar, in contrast to the behavior observed during the first cycle, shown in Figure 6.

This suggests that, in this coexistence setting, after the initial transient dynamics, the pattern formation process may become periodic in time, synchronized with the environmental periodicity. Successive instability intervals give rise to highly structured aggregations, which are followed by stable phases during which spatial heterogeneity is substantially reduced and the dynamics of the system are driven by those of the non-diffusive and non-chemotactic ODE system (10).

We next turn to study the behavior of the system under non-synchronous carrying capacities, to investigate the changes produced in the instability sets.

4.1.2 Example II: Out-of-phase carrying capacities

To study the dynamics of system (6) under non-synchronous carrying capacities, we next consider the following parameters

a1=0.3,a2=0.15,μ1=1,μ2=2.5α=1,β=1,χ2=2,1+f1(t)=1−0.3sin(0.25t),1+f2(t)=1+0.3sin(0.25t),\begin{gathered}a_{1}=0.3,\quad a_{2}=0.15,\quad\mu_{1}=1,\quad\mu_{2}=2.5\quad\alpha=1,\quad\beta=1,\\[6.45831pt] \chi_{2}=2,\quad 1+f_{1}(t)=1-0.3\sin(0.25t),\quad 1+f_{2}(t)=1+0.3\sin(0.25t)\,,\end{gathered} (49)

where the carrying capacities 1+f1​(t)1+f_{1}(t) and 1+f2​(t)1+f_{2}(t) are out of phase, and the maxima of one coincide with the minima of the other. In the previous biological interpretation, one can think of two distinct phenotypes, adapted to opposite seasonal conditions. The purpose of this example is to analyze the location of each instability set and, as previously anticipated —and contrary to what Figure 4 could suggest— conclude that these need not coincide with the maxima of each of the carrying capacities.

As in Example I, it is direct to check that the parameter set (49) satisfies conditions (18), ensuring the existence of a unique, globally attracting, coexistence solution (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}) to system (10). Moreover, through a numerical integration, one can check that for such state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}), hypothesis (12) does also hold, granting the unique solvability of equations (32) for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. By computing the solutions χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) and χ^1(k)​(t)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{\,(k)}(t), we obtain that in this case

χcrit=χ^c(17)≈3.2116\chi_{\text{crit}}=\widehat{\chi}_{c}^{\,(17)}\approx 3.2116

This time, we select for instance χ1=5>χcrit\chi_{1}=5>\chi_{\text{crit}}, which yields the following instability sets

ℐ1=[0,3.536)∪(10.229,8​π],ℐ2=[0,3.915)∪(10.861,8​π],\mathcal{I}_{1}=[0,3.536)\cup(10.229,8\pi],\quad\mathcal{I}_{2}=[0,3.915)\cup(10.861,8\pi], (50)

with very similar values. It therefore follows that

ℐ=ℐ1∪ℐ2=[0,3.915)∪(10.229,8​π].\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\mathcal{I}_{2}=[0,3.915)\cup(10.229,8\pi]. (51)

The extended instability sets ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)}, obtained through (50), are represented in Figure 8, together with the carrying capacities 1+f1​(t)1+f_{1}(t) and 1+f2​(t)1+f_{2}(t), as well as the periodic coexistence state (u~,v~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}).

As it can be seen, and as indicated by (50), the instability sets for uu and vv are very similar in terms of their temporal location. However, this contrasts with the out-of-phase behavior exhibited by u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v}, as a result of the non-synchronized carrying capacities 1+f11+f_{1} and 1+f21+f_{2}. In particular, on the top panel, the complement set [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(1)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)}, represented in green, is concentrated around the minima of the carrying capacity 1+f1​(t)1+f_{1}(t). Consequently, linear stability may occur only under relatively unfavorable environmental conditions for the first species, while instability arises when the carrying capacity is large enough. In contrast, the bottom panel reveals a markedly different situation, as the green regions, now corresponding to [0,∞)∖ℐ∞(2)[0,\infty)\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)}, are located near the maxima of 1+f2​(t)1+f_{2}(t), where environmental conditions are most favorable for the second species.

Hence, as previously anticipated, instability is not necessarily associated with intervals in which the carrying capacities attain sufficiently large values, promoting population growth. In fact, the dynamics of vv in this example reveal the complete opposite. Indeed, the location of these instability sets is not determined exclusively by ecological favorability, and instead follows from a more intricate mechanism rooted in the geometry of χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)}, as will be further discussed in Section 5.1.

To conclude this example, using initial data (48) —the same values used in Example I— we numerically solve system (6) with parameters (49) and χ1=5>χcrit\chi_{1}=5>\chi_{\text{crit}}. This results in the plots shown in Figure 9, where, as in Figure 5, the comparative between (u,v,w)(u,v,w) and (u~,v~,w~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}) is represented.

As in Figure 5, we find that both species exhibit a cyclic aggregation–homogenization behavior, marked by the instability intervals ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)}. After an initial regime in which the solution remains close to the spatially homogeneous state, the first aggregates emerge during a relatively short time interval, approximately between t=20t=20 and t=30t=30. This is followed by recurrent stages of spatial homogenization and aggregation. In contrast with the spatial patterns obtained in Figure 5, the structures that arise in this case remain comparatively stationary after the first two environmental cycles, exhibiting only minor temporal variations before rapidly dissipating near the end of each instability interval.

4.2 Competitive exclusion

After the previous two examples, in which the ODE system (10) admitted a unique positive and globally attracting coexistence state as a result of (18), we now investigate the competitive exclusion scenario. We select a parameter set for which (19) holds, and consequently the unique global attractor of system (10) is the semitrivial state (u~​(t),0)\big(\tilde{u}(t),0\big), where u~\tilde{u} is the unique positive and T−T-periodic solution to the nonautonomous logistic equation

u′=μ1​u​(1+f1​(t)−u),t>0.u^{\prime}=\mu_{1}u\big(1+f_{1}(t)-u\big),\quad t>0.

4.2.1 Example III: Semitrivial periodic state

In order to compare the results with those obtained in the coexistence scenario, we select the same domain Ω=(0,50)\Omega=(0,50) and parameters from Example I, except for a2a_{2}, which we suitably modify so that (19) is satisfied. In this way, we consider

a1=0.25,a2=4,μ1=1,μ2=2.5,α=1,β=0.8,χ2=1.5,1+f1(t)=1−0.6sin(0.25t),1+f2(t)=1−0.5sin(0.25t).\begin{gathered}a_{1}=0.25,\quad a_{2}=4,\quad\mu_{1}=1,\quad\mu_{2}=2.5,\quad\alpha=1,\quad\beta=0.8,\\[6.45831pt] \chi_{2}=1.5,\quad 1+f_{1}(t)=1-0.6\sin(0.25t),\quad 1+f_{2}(t)=1-0.5\sin(0.25t)\,.\end{gathered} (52)

This time, the very high competition rate a2=4a_{2}=4 implies that

1+f2M=1.5≤4⋅0.4=a2​(1+f1L),1+f_{2}^{M}=1.5\leq 4\cdot 0.4=a_{2}(1+f_{1}^{L}),

and as a result system (10) cannot sustain a population of the second species that does not eventually become extinct. Computing u~\tilde{u}, one can verify that the solvability assumption (12) holds for v~≡0\tilde{v}\equiv 0.

We recall that, as asserted by Lemma 3.3, in the competitive exclusion case, 𝒬^k​(χ1,t)>0\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}(\chi_{1},t)>0 for all k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, all t>0t>0 and all χ1∈ℝ\chi_{1}\in\mathbb{R}. Consequently, the instability analysis reduces to the study of χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t), since there are no thresholds associated with 𝒬^k\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k}. Computing the functions χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) for k∈{1,…,30}k\in\{1,\dots,30\}, we represent the results in Figure 10, only showing the same subset of modes as in Figure 2. This time, the value of χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}} is given by

χcrit=χc(18)≈3.202,\chi_{\text{crit}}=\chi_{c}^{(18)}\approx 3.202,

which is also represented in Figure 10 in gray dashed line in the central and right-hand panels. As in Example I, we consider χ1=6>χcrit\chi_{1}=6>\chi_{\text{crit}}, depicted in black dashed line.

Comparing the plots of χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) with those on the top panel of Figure 2, corresponding to the periodic coexistence case, we observe a very similar qualitative behavior. In particular, for each fixed mode kk, the temporal profiles have essentially the same shape, with the main difference however lying in their magnitude. Throughout the range of modes considered, the values of χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) are consistently lower in the competitive exclusion case. For example, the maximum of χ1(1)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(1)}(t) in Figure 10 is below 350350, compared with approximately 375375 in the coexistence case from Figure 2, while for k=6k=6, in Figure 10 we find χ1(6)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(6)}(t) uniformly below 1212, whereas it attains values close to 1414 in Figure 2. This difference is due to the combination of contribution of v~\tilde{v} in the coexistence case, which vanishes in the current competitive exclusion scenario, and the effect of the higher value of a2a_{2}.

This further influences the critical threshold for instability χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}, given in this case by 3.2023.202, which is slightly less than 3.2873.287, obtained for the coexistence case. Consequently, in the present example, where the two parameter sets differ only in the value of a2a_{2}, this indicates that increasing the competitive effect of the first species on the second lowers the chemotactic sensitivity required for transient instability.

With the chosen value of χ1=6>χcrit\chi_{1}=6>\chi_{\text{crit}}, the instability set is given by

ℐ=ℐ1=[0,4.925)∪(8.083,25.132].\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}_{1}=[0,4.925)\cup(8.083,25.132]. (53)

As in the previous examples, we represent the extended instability set ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)}, together with the carrying capacity 1+f1​(t)1+f_{1}(t) and the periodic component u~​(t)\tilde{u}(t) of the unique global attractor to system (10) in Figure 11. The corresponding quantities associated with the second species are omitted, since in the case of competitive exclusion, the sufficient instability criterion does not detect instability of the trivial component.

This time, as Figure 4 showed for Example I, the only possible regimes of stability are located in a neighborhood of the minima of the carrying capacity of 1+f11+f_{1}, while for sufficiently large carrying capacities, instability holds.

Lastly, using this value of χ1=6>χcrit\chi_{1}=6>\chi_{\text{crit}} and parameters (52), we solve the complete PDE system (6) with initial data

u⁡(x,0)=u~​(0)+ε​sin⁡(π​x/50),v⁡(x,0)=v~​(0)+ε​|cos⁡(π​x/50)|=ε​|cos⁡(π​x/50)|,u(x,0)=\tilde{u}(0)+\varepsilon\sin(\pi x/50),\quad v(x,0)=\tilde{v}(0)+\varepsilon\big|\hskip-1.42271pt\cos(\pi x/50)\big|=\varepsilon\big|\hskip-1.42271pt\cos(\pi x/50)\big|, (54)

for ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05. We remark that these are the same initial data considered in (49), except for the fact that the perturbation in v⁡(x,0)v(x,0) is considered in absolute value to preserve the nonnegativity of the solution. The evolution plots are represented in Figure 12, showing the comparative between (u,v,w)(u,v,w) and (u~,v~,w~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}).

The most substantial difference with respect to the previous examples is observed in the vv component of the solution. The initial perturbation rapidly decays, as a result of the strong competitive effect exerted by the first species, and consequently the center panel shows essentially no discrepancies between vv and v~\tilde{v}. We recall that, in the competitive exclusion case, Lemma 3.3 ensures the positivity of 𝒬^k\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}_{k} for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, preventing the application of the sufficient instability criterion from Lemma 3.1 to the modal amplitudes of the perturbations of vv. Although this does not rule out the possibility of instability, for the present parameter set, perturbations of the excluded species decay rapidly, so that competitive exclusion is maintained despite the transient instability exhibited by the first species.

With respect to uu and ww, transient aggregation patterns once again develop, illustrating the cyclic behavior, alternating heterogeneous aggregations phases —occurring during the extended instability set— with periods of spatial homogeneity, where perturbations decay. Despite their overall symmetry, the resulting patterns are less regular than those observed in Figures 5 and 9, exhibiting thinner aggregates that attain considerably higher population densities. In particular, the density of the first species exceeds 5, substantially above the values obtained in Example I, despite the same parameters (and particularly the same chemotactic sensitivity) being considered for both uu and ww. This difference can be attributed to the competitive exclusion of the second species, which removes the interspecific competition acting on the first one and allows it to concentrate more strongly within the aggregation regions.

5 Further remarks

Lastly, we collect here some final observations concerning the results from the previous examples.

5.1 On the location of the instability sets

Despite what Figure 4 in Example I might suggest, and as illustrated by Figure 8 in Example II, the location of the instability sets is not directly tied to the times at which the carrying capacities attain their maxima. Instead, for a fixed value of χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}} the instability sets ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} and ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} are fundamentally determined by the geometry of the threshold functions χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)}, whose shape ultimately depends on the coefficients aka_{k}, bkb_{k} and b^k\widehat{b}_{k} introduced in Lemma 3.2.

In particular, one important observation can be made with respect to aka_{k} and the role of hypothesis (12). From (35), we have that

ak​(t)=u~​(t)​λk1+λk​[−α​λk+μ2​(α⁡(1+f2​(t))−G⁡(t))],a_{k}(t)=\tilde{u}(t)\frac{\lambda_{k}}{1+\lambda_{k}}\Big[-\alpha\lambda_{k}+\mu_{2}\big(\alpha(1+f_{2}(t))-G(t)\big)\Big],

where

G⁡(t):=α​a2​u~​(t)+(2​α−a2​β)​v~​(t)G(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\alpha a_{2}\tilde{u}(t)+\left(2\alpha-a_{2}\beta\right)\tilde{v}(t)

As previously discussed, assumption (12) implies that α⁡(1+f2​(t))−G⁡(t)<0\alpha(1+f_{2}(t))-G(t)<0 for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], ensuring that ak​(t)a_{k}(t) remains uniformly negative over [0,T][0,T]. Furthermore, for each fixed mode k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}, the temporal profile of aka_{k} —and consequently those of χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)}— is largely dependent on that of G⁡(t)G(t). Coefficients α​a2\alpha a_{2} and 2​α−a2​β2\alpha-a_{2}\beta can therefore be understood as two weights, determining the relative contribution of u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v} to G⁡(t)G(t)

In Example I, as the carrying capacities were in phase, the periodic coexistence states u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v} inherit an essentially similar behavior, as Figure 4 shows. Hence, the weighted sum G⁡(t)G(t) preserves this common temporal structure, and its extrema are therefore aligned with those of 1+f21+f_{2}, as depicted in Figure 1. Similarly, since the time dependence of the coefficients bkb_{k} and b^k\widehat{b}_{k} is expressed only through u~\tilde{u}, v~\tilde{v} and the carrying capacities fif_{i}, the threshold functions χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)}, which by (36) are given by

χ1(k)​(t)=−bk​(t)ak​(t),χ^1(k)=−b^k​(t)ak​(t),\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t)=-\frac{b_{k}(t)}{a_{k}(t)},\quad\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)}=-\frac{\widehat{b}_{k}(t)}{a_{k}(t)},

inherit essentially the same temporal phase. Consequently, the instability sets (47) were concentrated around the maxima of the periodic states.

In Example II, the out-of-phase carrying capacities lead to a markedly different behavior. As shown in Figure 8, the instability set of uu remains concentrated around the maxima of u~\tilde{u}, whereas that of vv is now located near the minima of v~\tilde{v} . This time, for the parameter set (49), the weighted sum takes the form

G⁡(t)=0.15​u~​(t)+1.85​v~​(t),G(t)=0.15\tilde{u}(t)+1.85\tilde{v}(t),

and thus its behavior is dominated by the contribution of v~\tilde{v}. Since the phase shift in the carrying capacity 1+f21+f_{2} reverses the oscillatory behavior of v~\tilde{v} with respect to Example I, the same phase reversal is inherited by G⁡(t)G(t), and consequently by the dominant contribution to the coefficient aka_{k}. As a result, the threshold functions attain their smallest values near the minima of v~\tilde{v}, leading to instability intervals concentrated around these times.

In this way, G⁡(t)G(t) provides a mechanism for controlling the temporal location of the instability intervals. A further important observation is that the geometry of GG is not determined only by the weights, but also by the magnitude of the coexistence states u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v}. In Example II, as both carrying capacities attained the same maximum and minimum values, and competition between both species was mild, the magnitude of both states u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v} was similar, as Figure 8 shows. However, if one species experiences a much stronger competitive pressure or significantly less favorable environmental conditions, its population may remain comparatively small, reducing its influence on G⁡(t)G(t), even when its associated weight is relatively large.

As a result, by suitably balancing the weights in G⁡(t)G(t) and the amplitudes of u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v}, while simultaneously ensuring that hypothesis (12) holds, one can obtain a wider variety of instability distributions. In particular, the extrema of G⁡(t)G(t) need not coincide with those of either carrying capacity. To illustrate this behavior, we consider the following parameter values

a1=0,a2=0.3,μ1=3,μ2=0.25,α=4,β=2.5,χ2=1.5,1+f1(t)=1.4−0.4sin(0.25t),1+f2(t)=0.7+0.1sin(0.25t),\begin{gathered}a_{1}=0,\quad a_{2}=0.3,\quad\mu_{1}=3,\quad\mu_{2}=0.25,\quad\alpha=4,\quad\beta=2.5,\\[6.45831pt] \chi_{2}=1.5,\quad 1+f_{1}(t)=1.4-0.4\sin(0.25t),\quad 1+f_{2}(t)=0.7+0.1\sin(0.25t),\end{gathered} (55)

again with out-of-phase carrying capacities. In this case, the combination of the absence of interspecific competition exerted by the second species (a1=0)(a_{1}=0) and the fact that 1+f1​(t)1+f_{1}(t) lies substantially above 1+f2​(t)1+f_{2}(t) for all times, results in u~\tilde{u} attaining significantly higher values than v~\tilde{v}, as shown on the top panel of Figure 13. Consequently, although here G⁡(t)=1.2​u~​(t)+7.25​v~​(t)G(t)=1.2\tilde{u}(t)+7.25\tilde{v}(t), the larger magnitude of u~\tilde{u} together with the comparatively small amplitude of the oscillations of v~\tilde{v} cause the phase of G⁡(t)G(t) to lie closer to that of 1+f1​(t)1+f_{1}(t) than of 1+f2​(t)1+f_{2}(t). This is represented in the bottom panel of Figure 13, where G⁡(t)G(t) is plotted in blue, together with α​(1+f2​(t))\alpha(1+f_{2}(t)) in red. As it can be seen, this shift of phase in G⁡(t)G(t) makes the inequality in hypothesis (12) tighter.

Parameter values (55) yield χcrit=0.588\chi_{\text{crit}}=0.588. Selecting for instance χ1=1.05>χcrit\chi_{1}=1.05>\chi_{\text{crit}}, produces the instability intervals depicted in Figure 14. As it can be seen, the extended instability intervals ℐ∞(1)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(1)} and ℐ∞(2)\mathcal{I}_{\infty}^{(2)} now contain both, the maxima and minima of the carrying capacities. Moreover, the complement sets, where linear stability may occur, correspond to values of the carrying capacities for which instability is also observed at other times within the same environmental cycle. Hence, identical values of the carrying capacities may be associated with either instability or possible stability, depending on the stage of the environmental cycle at which they are attained.

This shows that instability is not determined by the instantaneous value of the carrying capacities alone, but also by the temporal interaction between the environmental forcing and the periodic coexistence state, mediated through the weighted function G⁡(t)G(t).

5.2 Negative instability thresholds

Lastly, we devote a few lines to discuss the possibility of negative instability thresholds. Despite all the previous examples yielding positive values of χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}, such positivity is not guaranteed for arbitrary parameter values.

For the threshold functions χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)} defined in (36), hypothesis (12) only ensures that ak​(t)<0a_{k}(t)<0 for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. However, the signs of χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} and χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)} —and consequently that of χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}— depend naturally on the coefficients bkb_{k} and b^k\widehat{b}_{k}. Without additional assumptions, these coefficients need not remain positive throughout [0,T][0,T].

In particular, if there exists k∈ℕ+k\in\mathbb{N}^{+} such that bk​(t)b_{k}(t) or b^k​(t)\widehat{b}_{k}(t) become negative for some t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], then χcrit<0\chi_{\text{crit}}<0. Consequently, heterogeneous aggregations may arise when the first species is non-chemotactic, or even when it undergoes repulsive taxis, which is generally a further stabilizing mechanism. In such situations, the instability can be understood as being driven by the attractive chemotactic response of the second species, whose influence is sufficient to destabilize the homogeneous state despite the absence of attracting taxis in the first species.

As an example, we consider the following parameters

a1=0.4,a2=0.4,μ1=3,μ2=0.7,α=5,β=7,χ2=1.5,1+f1(t)=3−0.5sin(0.25t),1+f2(t)=1−0.5cos(0.25t).\begin{gathered}a_{1}=0.4,\quad a_{2}=0.4,\quad\mu_{1}=3,\quad\mu_{2}=0.7,\quad\alpha=5,\quad\beta=7,\\[6.45831pt] \chi_{2}=1.5,\quad 1+f_{1}(t)=3-0.5\sin(0.25t),\quad 1+f_{2}(t)=1-0.5\cos(0.25t).\end{gathered} (56)

The left panel on Figure 15 shows the plots of χ1(k)​(t)\chi_{1}^{(k)}(t) and χ^1(k)​(t)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)}(t), for k∈{5,…,10}k\in\{5,\dots,10\}. The values of χ1(k)\chi_{1}^{(k)} are plotted in solid lines, while χ^1(k)\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(k)} are represented in dashed lines. As it can be seen, for each kk, the values on both graphs are very similar, in particular attaining negative values. This results in the negative threshold

χcrit=χ^1(5)​(5.05)=−9.72<0.\chi_{\text{crit}}=\widehat{\chi}_{1}^{(5)}(5.05)=-9.72<0.

To illustrate the patterns generated for χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}} the right panel of Figure 15 depicts two representative solution profiles, the first computed for χ1=−6<0\chi_{1}=-6<0, shown on the top row, and the second one for χ1=0\chi_{1}=0, on the bottom row.

In both cases, we obtain highly structured and nearly symmetric patterns. In the repulsive taxis case, the minima of uu coincide with the maxima of ww, reflecting the chemorepulsive response of the first species. In contrast, these regions of high chemoattractant concentration promote the aggregation of the second species vv, due to the attraction caused by the positive sensitivity χ2>0\chi_{2}>0.

A similar behavior is observed in the taxis–free scenario, where only the second species is chemotactically attracted to ww, while the first species evolves solely through diffusion, logistic growth, and interspecific competition. Although uu no longer exhibits chemorepulsion, its minima are again located at the maxima of ww. In this case, however, the mechanism is different. In particular the high concentrations of ww attract the second species, leading to aggregations of vv, which in turn suppress the first species through interspecific competition.

We stress, however, that the instability mechanism remains fundamentally chemotactically driven. Indeed, if both sensitivities vanish, that is, χ1=χ2=0\chi_{1}=\chi_{2}=0, the result in [2] rules out the possibility of instability. Consequently, cases with χcrit≤0\chi_{\text{crit}}\leq 0 should not be interpreted as pattern formation in the absence of chemotaxis. Rather, they reflect that the attractive chemotactic response of the second species alone is already sufficient to destabilize the spatially homogeneous state, even when the first species is non-chemotactic or repelled by the chemoattractant.

6 Discussion and conclusions

Throughout this work, we investigated the rise of recurrent aggregations in the two–species chemotaxis–competition system (6), which features periodic environmental conditions. Our aim was to derive a threshold for χ1\chi_{1}, the chemotactic sensitivity of the first species, that leads to transient linear instability of the spatially homogeneous state (u~​(t),v~​(t),w~​(t))\big(\tilde{u}(t),\tilde{v}(t),\tilde{w}(t)\big), obtained through the ODE system (10). This results in an opposite behavior to that studied in [32], where it was shown that sufficiently large logistic growth rates μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} guarantee convergence of all solutions of (6) to (u~,v~,w~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}). In contrast, the present work identifies parameter regimes in which transient linear instability and recurrent aggregation may occur.

In this way, our main analytical result is Theorem 1.1, which provides a way to compute the critical threshold χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}. In particular, for any χ1>χcrit\chi_{1}>\chi_{\text{crit}}, there exists a set of times ℐ⊂[0,T]\mathcal{I}\subset[0,T], over which the spatially homogeneous state (u~,v~,w~)(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}) becomes linearly unstable.

Particularly interesting dynamics arise whenever [0,T]∖ℐ[0,T]\setminus\mathcal{I} is not empty, as due to the environmental periodicity, the instability becomes recurrent over the subsequent environmental cycles. In particular, the examples in Section 3 showed the alternation of stable and unstable intervals, over which spatial perturbations grow and decay, resulting in transient aggregations. This interplay between homogenization and destabilization is clearly visible in the plots shown in Figures 5 and 9, in the case of periodic coexistence, and Figure 12 in a competitive exclusion scenario.

Some final remarks were made in Section 5 concerning the location of the instability sets and the possibility of negative thresholds for χ1\chi_{1}. In particular, the example constructed through parameters (55) showed how instability is not directly tied to instantaneous values of the carrying capacities, and in fact the same value of a carrying capacity may correspond either to stability or to instability, depending on the stage of the environmental cycle. With respect to negative values of χcrit\chi_{\text{crit}}, parameter set (56) produced the results shown in Figure 15, generating patterns in taxis–free and even chemorepulsive scenarios.

We emphasize that the instability mechanism considered throughout this work is fundamentally chemotactically driven, as remarked at the end of Section 4. While the ecological quantities 1+fi1+f_{i}, u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v} determine the conditions under which instability arises, the underlying destabilizing mechanism remains chemotactic.

Finally, we note that the instability criterion developed in this work is based on the sufficient condition from Lemma 3.1. Consequently, although it provides a practical framework for detecting transient instability, it cannot be used to conclude linear stability. Moreover, the present analysis is entirely linear and therefore concerns only the onset of pattern formation. While the examples showed that it successfully predicts the emergence of transient aggregations and their temporal location, it does not provide information on the nonlinear evolution of the patterns, their shape or the interactions between aggregates once instability has developed.
